questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were too many universities to choose from so I had to narrow it down somehow. The first restriction was to choose something outside of Europe. Secondly, I thought North America might be a cool place to study and I wasn't really attracted to the US. So Canada it was. McGill had a really nice selection of courses so that was the main reason to go there. And of course also to experience Montreal, visit nearby cities and go hiking and skiing in the surrounding nature.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: This wasn't at problem at all. As far as I remember, at least.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were some nice orientation events in the first week with academic advice and information and information on the social clubs at McGill.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I was offered a shared apartment in a student residence (Solin Hall) 3 km from campus.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: When living in a McGill residence the meal plan is mandatory. And it is way too expensive. The total cost for the meal plan was 1300 CAD which you have to spend in the dining halls and cafes on campus. There are some decent cafes and a single good coffee place but in general it is pretty overpriced. If you choose to live in a student residence and get the meal plan I would recommend that you try out all the food places on campus in the first two week so you don't end up spending all your meal plan money at RVC (by far the worst dining hall on campus, but for some bewildering reason also the most popular).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It is the easiest and least stressful way to find housing in Montreal so in this regard it was pretty nice. However, it is also the most expensive option. Paying 1150 CAD a month for housing hurts. Plus, there was nothing in the apartment when we arrived besides some furniture. We had to buy everything ourself; pots, pans, plates, cutlery, everything.  But it is also a really nice and easy way to meet new people and get friends from day one. I was lucky to get a flatmate that quickly became a very good friend and I ended up spending a lot of time with him. McGill chose to gather most of the exchange students in the same residence which was pretty nice. This meant that you lived with other exchange students and not 18 year old first year students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was a bit stressfull having to write the professors and departments to be allowed to register for the courses. Also, it was annoying that the course registration opened earlier for the local students then for the exchange students. This meant that some courses was full before we were allowed to register. However, in the end I still managed to get the courses I wanted. You just have to check several times a day if a seat opens.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Just the basics on how to register. The virtual schedule builder was helpful, though.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I managed to get all the courses I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you haven't been able to register for the course, just attend the first class of the semester in the add-drop period and talk with the professor. He might let you in to the course.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was pretty similar to back home, maybe a bit easier.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There were way more presentations, essays and small assignments than back home. However, the grading for these things were pretty chill. You could easily get away with making a mediocre essay or presentation and still get a good grade. At least in the courses I followed. I ended up with quite a stressfull November because most of my essays and presentation were due there. So maybe think about this when you choose your courses - I didn't. But then at least my September, first part og October and December were easy.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
PHGY488 Stem Cell Biology 
PHGY524 Chronobiology
BIOL544 Genetic Basis of Lifespan
WCOM314 Communicating Science

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would highly recommend Chronobiology and Genetic Basis of Lifespan. Both courses were taught by amazing professors. Genetic Basis of Lifespan was also very chill in terms of workload. Just one class a week, one presentation and one essay. No midterm of final exam. However, the workload in Chronobiology was pretty high - but definitely worth it. Stem Cell Biology might be the worst course I've ever had. Just an unstructured course with poor teaching. Communicating Science was not bad. It reminded me quite a lot of danish classes in high school. I'm not sure I learned that much from the course, but it was pretty chill and kind of fun from time to time.

questions.answer: Overall it is just way more expensive to live in Montreal than I thought.

questions.answer: Pretty much everything was more expensive than I thought.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Pretty much everything

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I joined a running club (McGill Olympic Club) that I really enjoyed. There were trainings two times a week with a coach and sometimes we also met Saturday for a longer run. All levels could join the club, so no try-out for this one.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: First of all, enjoy Montreal - just walk around the city, go to the Islands, go to Mont Royal. But also make sure to visit the surrounding nature and cities. Rent a car an go hiking - there a good places within a two hour drive. And then Toronto with the CN tower and Niagara Falls close by is a must.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join a club. And maybe choose courses with fewer students. It's easier to socialize this way than in large lectures.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The city is build for cars, not bikes.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Montreal and McGill are just way more multicultural than Copenhagen and KU.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Go travel as much as you can as early as possible. The semester might hit you in the face and demand a lot of studying later on so use your freedom in the beginning. And also, lower your academic ambitions so you have time to do other things. And join a club - this was one of the best things I did and really helped me to get a wonderful daily life in Montreal.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember you don't have the get the International Health Insurance. You can apply for the RAMQ when you arrive which is free of charge. You don't have to pay full price for the metro card. Although McGill says that you have to be enrolled for the full year to get a reduced fare metro card there are a way to get around that. La Banquise is the only place you can get an acceptable poutine. All other places it is close to disgusting.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing how fast you can adapt and feel at home in a new country and a new city. Meeting people from all around the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: How expensive it was.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
